newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala government, rebels to renew peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala government, rebels to renew peace talks.

text.p: The government of Guatemala and leftist guerrillas said on Thursday they would resume peace talks aimed at putting an end to Latin America's longest-running civil war.

The two sides issued simultaneous statements saying conditions were right for a return to negotiations, which broke off on Oct. 28 when it was discovered that a rebel commando had kidnapped a wealthy elderly woman for ransom.
The guerrilla commander of the faction that committed the kidnapping announced on Thursday he would withdraw from the talks, apparently clearing the way for them to begin anew.
"President Alvaro Arzu has decided that indispensible political conditions exist for a return to the negotiating table," the government's Public Relations Ministry said in a statement.

Meanwhile the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) said in a statement issued from its Mexico City office that rebel commanders "believe that the acceptable conditions have been created in order to continue peace talks."
Neither side said when the U.N.-brokered negotiations might resume, nor whether a final peace agreement could be signed by December as previously planned.
The 36-year-old armed conflict is the last in Central America. More than 100,000 people, mostly civilians, have died and more than 40,000 are missing.

The talks, which have taken place most recently at a Mexico City hotel, were abruptly suspended after it was discovered that a rebel commando had kidnapped an elderly woman belonging to the influential family that owns Guatemala's only cement company.
Olga de Novella was abducted from her wheelchair while leaving church after her bodyguards were overpowered. She was released in exchange for the freedom of a guerrilla commander who was in jail.
The URNG has long kidnapped people for ransom to finance its insurrection, but pledged to end such practices under preliminary agreements reached with the government.
The guerrilla command said it disapproved of the kidnapping but assumed political responsibility for it.

Rebel commander Rodrigo Asturias (alias Commander Gaspar Ilom), one of the chief guerrilla negotiatiors, said in a separate statement that he would resign from the talks "as a gesture on my part" to get them back on track.
Asturias leads the Organisation of People in Arms (ORPA) faction that carried out the kidnapping.

"I am aware of the situation created by the kidnapping of Mrs. Novella has meant a blow to the credibility of the peace process and affected the climate of confidence between the parties," Asturias said.
